title: SpaceNEXT 2026 | The FCC's Role in the New Space Economy
transcriptText:
Good morning. I want to start with a
confession. When most people hear FCC,
they think of two things: broadcast TV
and robo calls.
Maybe three things if you include a
wardrobe malfunction.
So, I understand if FCC and space
economy sound like they don't belong in
the same sentence, but they do and
that's the story I want to tell today.
Just take a look at these numbers.
613
billion dollars. That's the global space
economy in 2024, not the future,
right now.
There are over 15,000 satellites in
orbit. We set a record last year with
300 and
uh 24 launches and nearly 80% of this
activity is driven by the private
sector.
And among the private sector, American
companies dominate.
65% of the launch market, 83% of the
commercial satellites built, 70% of the
world's satellites operated. This is not
a niche industry anymore. It's a pillar
of the eco- American economy and it's
growing fast. And that's why we're
having this event here today.
So, where does the FCC fit in?
Let me walk you through it.
The FCC's authority in space rests on
four pillars.
First, preventing harmful interference.
Every satellite, whether or not it
provides
communication services to the public,
needs radio frequencies or spectrum to
work. And the FCC makes sure that those
those signals don't step on each other.
The second is efficient spectrum use.
Spectrum is finite, it's valuable. We
can't let anybody waste it or hoard it.
Third, national security.
We coordinate with federal agencies that
have equities in national security, like
the Department of Defense, to make sure
that satellite systems don't threaten
the country.
And then finally, space safety. Orbital
debris is a real problem.
These are legitimate pillars.
The question is
whether our rules have kept pace with
the industry. And let me give you a
spoiler, they hadn't.
Here's what the journey looks like for a
satellite operator who wants an FCC
license.
You file an application, a public notice
goes out, there's a period for public
comment, there's a security review
potentially, a technical review,
and maybe you'll get a decision.
Now, so far so good. All of those steps
sound eminently reasonable.
The problem is what happens between
them.
Satellite operators book launch vehicles
years in advance.
They raise capital based on projected
timelines. If a license is delayed, the
launch window passes, investors get
nervous, competitors gain ground.
And a single year of delay on a 500
million dollar program can mean 100
million dollars in lost revenue.
Time is money
and in space,
time is a lot of money.
Let me put this in sharper terms.
Regulatory delay imperils financing.
Delay means missed launch windows.
Rebooking a launch can cost tens of
millions of dollars or worse, you'll
lose your slot entirely.
And every day your satellite can't
operate is a day that you're not serving
customers and earning revenues.
And an FCC license isn't just a
permission, it's not just a piece of
paper.
It's a billion dollar strategic asset.
Amazon
invested 10 billion dollars
on the strength of its FCC license.
That's how much that piece of paper
matters.
Now, I want you to look at this chart.
In 2015, the FCC received about 40 space
station applications a year.
In 2024, that number was 300.
Plus
3,000 earth station applications. So,
our licensing system was built
for a 1990s era
geostationary satellite dominated
industry.
A world with just a handful of
satellites.
And just a few years ago, we found
ourselves drowning under the weight
of a space industrial revolution.
That's not an abstraction, by the way.
That delay is not uh a cost that didn't
materialize. It's broadband that didn't
reach rural communities. It's jobs that
didn't get created and innovation that
remained on the whiteboard.
That's real cost for everybody in this
room,
for this entire region,
for the entire American economy.
So, what exactly went wrong?
Well, let me give you the details.
Four core problems.
Number one, every application got a
bespoke review, even the routine ones.
The same technical analysis repeated
from scratch every single time.
Minor changes required major paperwork.
If you want to swap an antenna, that's a
full modification application.
If you want to adjust your power, well,
that that requires public comment. Our
technical rules, as I just mentioned,
were stuck in this 90s geostationary
era.
They assumed a world with just a couple
of big satellites, not thousands of
agile spacecraft using modern
beamforming technology.
And the pipeline, the actual plumbing of
our licensing system, just couldn't
handle the volume.
Now, let me give you my favorite example
of a well-intentioned rule going wrong.
The FCC had a rule that said you could
replace equipment on your earth station
without paperwork. That's good.
But only if the replacement was
electrically identical to what was
already there.
Uh that sounds reasonable, except when
technology moves forward, manufacturers
want to discontinue their products.
And electrically identical meant that
you just couldn't install a better
antenna without filing a full FCC
application. I want you to think about
that. We're penalizing operators for
upgrading their equipment. That makes no
sense.
We're punishing improvement. That also
makes no sense.
And it makes no sense because modern
satellites are using software-defined
radios. They get firmware updates over
the air.
Every update that changed an RF
characteristic required a new paperwork,
even if it didn't cause harmful
interference. It didn't increase that
risk.
It's like requiring a building permit
every time you update your phone.
That wasn't the only outdated rule,
there were others.
We have power restrictions from the 90s
called EPFD limits.
These are the most single constraining
requirement on non-geostationary
systems in orbit. I'll talk about more
of this in the second. We have
processing rounds where if you file an
application for a space system,
the FCC will put out a notice and call
the cattle bell and invite everybody to
come file. And then they process all of
those applications in batches, which
means that if you file an application,
you'd have to wait for years.
And then we have surety bonds that tied
up millions of dollars in capital that
hurt smaller players and new entrants.
And the revert the result was a perverse
set of outcomes.
one outcome that was really perverse is
what I'm going to call the backlog doom
loop. More applications led to more
delays, led to more amendments, led to
more applications and it fed on itself.
It the hole was growing faster than we
could dig out and we were digging really
hard.
The old system wasn't just slow, it was
getting slower.
All right, that that that's the problem.
Let me tell you about what we're doing
here at the FCC under Chairman Carr.
Everything that we're doing at the FCC
falls under four guiding principles.
Speed. We're clearing the backlog at a
record pace.
In 2025,
we reduced our earth station backlogs by
50%.
We're moving to shot clocks.
Simplicity.
We're replacing our rules with an
entirely new
uh rule set in our space modernization
initiative. Think of it as a licensing
assembly line, modular, predictable,
scalable. It's built for thousands of
Leo satellites, not the handful of Geos.
Security. We've launched a landmark
proceeding to protect GPS.
And spectrum abundance. We're looking to
release a historic amount of spectrum
for satellite broadband.
Now, we're taking care of the tur- first
two principles, speed and simplicity, in
one fell swoop.
And this is something that agencies
rarely do.
We looked at our satellite licensing
rules when we came in in 2025 and
realized it just wasn't going to work.
So,
we're going to tear it out root and
branch and we're going to replace it
with a 21st century era rule set.
No, you know, we're only going to do
both bespoke reviews when the
circumstances require it, but everything
else goes in the fast lane.
Let me Let me spend a moment on
security.
GPS is the invisible infrastructure of
modern life. Financial markets depend on
it for timing.
Agriculture depends on it for
precision farming.
But GPS disruptions can cost billions of
dollars.
And
uh cause
incalculable harm to the US economy. So,
what we did at the FCC is we launched a
dedicated proceeding to strengthen GPS
protections and explore backups,
alternatives, and complements to
position, navigation, and timing
capabilities.
I mentioned EPFD.
Um that's one part of our broader
spectrum agenda. But one thing that I'm
really excited about is we're looking at
opening up more than 20,000 MHz of
spectrum for satellite broadband. I want
to put that in context. 20,000 MHz is
more spectrum for satellite than is
available today for satellite broadband.
We're going to more than double that
amount.
And that matters because
satellite systems in low Earth orbit are
increasingly facing capacity
constraints. They're increasingly
becoming substitutes not only for the
broadband in your home but the broadband
on your phone.
More spectrum, more capacity, more
flexible rules brings technological
convergence. It allows satellite to
compete on the same footing as the fiber
that runs to your home
or the cellular frequencies that run to
your phone.
Now, let's talk about this EPFD issue.
It's what I think is potentially the
singest biggest unlock for satellite
broadband.
Updating these rules could increase the
capacity of LEOs in a particular area by
up to 700%.
And in the aggregate, it could increase
system capacity by up to 180%. Why? Why
is that the case?
Because it allows satellites to use
multiple beams to cover one area.
And that means more beams means more
capacity. It means you can load more
users
at the types of speeds that they expect
without running out of capacity.
And it's working. The things that we're
doing are delivering results.
I mentioned the 50% reduction in earth
station applications. We processed 85
satellite station applications, 900
earth station applications.
Six big ticket rule makings.
These aren't projections. These are
results.
And we're not doing it alone.
The industry support that we've received
has been remarkable.
The Satellite Industry Association,
CCIA, SpaceX, Amazon, Lockheed Martin,
AST.
These are companies that compete with
each other every day.
But on this issue, they're completely
aligned.
And when an industry as diverse as the
space economy speaks with one voice,
it's worth listening.
And Congress is listening, too.
Chairman Cruz and Senator Welch
introduced the SAT Streamlining Act.
It would codify a lot of the reforms
that we made at the FCC. Because while
we can reform our rules, they're not
permanent. They're always subject to
change in the future.
Congress thinks that this is an issue
that is important enough to hardwire
into the law.
So, let me leave you with five
takeaways.
First, the space economy is huge and
regulatory efficiency is a competitive
advantage not just for the companies,
but for the United States as it competes
against China and other uh nations that
seek to rival our space dominance. Two,
our legacy rules were built for a
different era. They created real costs
delaying financing, launch misses, and
unrealized innovation.
Three,
the FCC under Chairman Carr is executing
a transformation built on speed,
simplicity, security, and spectrum
abundance.
Four, industry support for what we're
doing is nearly unanimous.
Competitors agree.
Streamline predictable regulation is
essential.
Focus on the things that we need to
focus on, the real harms.
But don't put everything through a
bespoke review process. And five,
there's real interest in making our
reforms permanent.
I started with a confession.
The FCC and space, it seems like a
strange set of bedfellows.
But here's what I hope you take away
today.
The future is of space is not just about
rockets and satellites.
It's about the rules that govern them.
And if you get the rules right, you
unleash an industry. And if you get them
wrong, you hold that industry back.
And we are committed to getting the
rules right.
As Chairman Carr said,
you have committed partners at the FCC
who are doing everything we can to make
your next great big breakthroughs
possible.
Thank you for having me.
I have to leave, but I hope that you're
in touch. Please send me an email. Look
me up on LinkedIn. I hope to connect
with all of you. Thank you again.
>> [applause]
